archetype.name: Playoff Team (defense-first)
archetype.definition: A second-year Macdonald team whose elite, explosive-proof defense and strong special teams carry an offense that runs too often, gives the ball away and has changed quarterbacks repeatedly.

report.headline: An elite defense dragging a turnover-prone, run-stubborn offense toward a wild-card spot
report.take:
Seattle is 6-4 and the record undersells it slightly. The point differential implies 6.9 wins and winsOverExpected sits at -0.94, so this is a team that has played a bit better than its record. That is a reversal from last year's 14-3 run, which leaned on luck at +3.29 wins over expected. What carried over from 2025 is the defense. It ranked 1st in EPA allowed last season and is 5th now, 2nd in success rate allowed and 1st in yards allowed. In Macdonald's second year, that unit is the identity, not a fluke.

The defense works by taking away the big play. Opponents hit explosive passes on 4.5% of dropbacks, the lowest rate in the league, and deep-ball EPA allowed is the best in football at -0.289. Kansas City managed 3 points, and Arizona was held to 7 and then 3. The cost of that shell is underneath and near the goal line. Short-pass EPA allowed ranks 25th, and opponents finish 75% of red-zone trips with touchdowns, 29th in the league. Seattle makes offenses earn every yard, then too often hands over the last few.

The offense is the problem, and the cause is mostly self-inflicted. The passing game is a respectable 12th in EPA per play. The run game is 30th, behind a line that allows pressure at the league's highest rate. Even so, Seattle passes 5.2 points less often than expected, 28th, so the play-calling keeps feeding its weakest unit. Turnovers have done the real damage: 16 giveaways and a -3 differential. Three of the four losses came with Drew Lock starting and coughing it up three or four times: Washington, San Francisco and Denver. Sam Darnold's starts have been cleaner, and Jaxon Smith-Njigba's 109 targets dwarf everyone else's no matter who throws.

The path forward depends on health more than talent. Darnold's quad, starting tackles Charles Cross and Abraham Lucas and guard Quenton Nelson all carry game-day return estimates. Those are hopes, not guarantees. The remaining schedule after San Francisco is friendly enough, with Dallas, the Giants, Philadelphia and Carolina, for this defense to bank a wild card. That holds only if the quarterback stops gifting possessions.

strengths.title: A defense that erases explosive plays
strengths.body: Seattle allows the fewest explosive passes and the best deep-ball EPA in the league, and it ranks 2nd in success rate allowed. This is a scheme-driven profile that also topped the league in 2025, so it is not a small-sample mirage. The interior losses of Leonard Williams and possibly Jarran Reed test the depth, but the coverage foundation should hold.

strengths.title: Pressure without blitz-dependence
strengths.body: A 25.7% pressure rate (5th) and the 3rd-best QB hit rate mean quarterbacks rarely get comfortable. That pressure is why third downs die at a 30.6% conversion rate. It travels week to week because it comes from the front, not from turnover luck.

strengths.title: Special teams as a hidden edge
strengths.body: Seattle adds 2.46 EPA a game on special teams, 5th in the league, which is worth real field position for a team that wins low-scoring games. Combined with a 100% fourth-down go rate in the right spots, the margins are being managed well.

concerns.title: Turnovers, especially with Lock
concerns.body: Sixteen giveaways have wiped out a solid takeaway count. The losses to Washington, San Francisco and Denver featured three, four and three turnovers. That is mostly a quarterback and protection problem rather than random luck, so it only fades if Darnold stays healthy.

concerns.title: Running into a broken run game
concerns.body: Rush EPA ranks 30th and run success 24th, yet Seattle passes well below expectation, 28th in pass rate over expected. With pass EPA a respectable 12th, the play mix is leaving value on the table. That is a choice that can change, but it hasn't yet.

concerns.title: Line leaking pressure, now short-handed
concerns.body: Seattle's quarterbacks face pressure at the highest rate in the league even with healthy starters, and Cross and Nelson are out with Lucas questionable. If backups are in, the problem that has fed the turnovers gets worse before it gets better.

trend.note: The defense has been consistent all season, holding four of the last five opponents to 13 or fewer. The offense swings with the quarterback and turnovers: a messy Lock stretch in late September and October gave way to cleaner wins over Kansas City, Arizona and Las Vegas.

nextGame.headline: Rematch at 9-1 San Francisco with Seattle's line in pieces
nextGame.body:
San Francisco is the best team on paper: 1st in net EPA, 1st in pass EPA and 1st in offensive success rate, behind a line that allows sacks on just 3.1% of dropbacks. The Week 5 meeting went 32-29 to the 49ers in Seattle, and Seattle's four turnovers and five sacks allowed were the difference. The 49ers' defense is lopsided. It is 1st against the run but only 16th in pass EPA allowed and dead last in sack rate. Their special teams rank last at -3.55 EPA a game, and a perfect one-score record plus +1.91 wins over expected suggests some fortune in that 9-1. The Book has San Francisco by 3, with Seattle at +154.

Availability is the swing. Darnold is listed out with a quad injury but suited up for an unofficial practice. Cross and Nelson are out and Lucas is questionable, all with game-day return estimates. On defense, Leonard Williams is out and Jarran Reed questionable. San Francisco lost right tackle Colton McKivitz for the season, linebacker Dre Greenlaw is out, Nate Hobbs is on IR, and starting corner Deommodore Lenoir is questionable with a foot injury. An early forecast shows drizzle and modest wind, worth a glance but nothing to build on yet.

waysToWin.title: Throw it, especially to Smith-Njigba
waysToWin.body: San Francisco's run defense is the league's best, while its pass defense is middling and it barely sacks anyone. Opposing WR1s have scored above their averages against it. Leaning on the pass instead of the usual run-heavy script gives Seattle its most efficient path, and Smith-Njigba's target share makes him the obvious engine.

waysToWin.title: Win the hidden yardage on special teams
waysToWin.body: Seattle ranks 5th in special teams EPA and San Francisco ranks last. In a game the Book sees as close, flipped field position and possibly points from the kicking game can cover for a shaky offense.

waysToWin.title: Pressure a reshuffled 49ers line
waysToWin.body: Without McKivitz, San Francisco's elite protection loses a starter. Seattle's pressure rate is 5th, and forcing Purdy off schedule is the best way to slow a passing game that ranks 1st in EPA. Making the 49ers drive the length of the field plays to a defense that allows almost nothing explosive.

waysToLose.title: Another turnover-fueled shootout loss
waysToLose.body: The first meeting turned on four Seattle giveaways. San Francisco ranks 5th in takeaways, and with backup tackles and possibly Lock under center, short fields for the league's top offense are the fastest way out of this game.

waysToLose.title: Death by short passes and red-zone sevens
waysToLose.body: Seattle's weak spots are short-pass defense and red-zone touchdowns allowed. A Shanahan offense that leads the league in success rate is built to dink down the field and finish. Holding them to field goals is the margin Seattle can't afford to lose.

waysToLose.title: Stubbornly running into the wall
waysToLose.body: If Seattle sticks to its run-first tendencies against the league's best run defense, it will face long third downs behind a depleted line. That is exactly how the protection failures and giveaways start.

nextGame.watch: Who starts at quarterback and tackle for Seattle: Darnold behind a healthy line changes this game, while Lock behind backups invites a repeat of Week 5.

restOfSeason.body:
The defense is the sustainable part. It was the league's best last year and is top-five again on efficiency, so expect opponents to keep landing in the high teens. Points allowed could creep up if the red-zone leaks persist, but that rate is unusually bad and should drift toward normal. The offense should also improve a little if Darnold stays healthy and the starting line returns, because the turnover rate in Lock's starts has been extreme. The record has slightly undershot the point differential, so a modest positive correction is fair to expect.

The schedule after San Francisco is favorable: Dallas has the league's worst defense, Philadelphia is 3-7, and the Giants and Carolina are beatable at or near home. The two games against the Rams, ranked 4th in defensive EPA, are the toughest left. The division title is likely out of reach with San Francisco at 9-1, so the realistic goal is a wild card. Seattle is well positioned for one if the giveaways shrink.
swingFactors: Darnold's quad and how often Lock has to start
Return of Cross, Nelson and Lucas on the line
Whether the play-calling shifts toward the pass

confidence.note: The defense has a two-year track record, but quarterback and offensive line health are unsettled.
